deep.reconstruction:
Setting: these notes try to characterise combinatorially which '1-dimensional' data come from a genuine '2-dimensional' arrangement of pseudolines in the projective plane, possibly non-simple. The 1-dimensional data are a set I of pseudolines, their incidences with the intersection points, and a 'polygonal structure' on each line, meaning the cyclic order of its points. For each triple J in beta_3(I) (3-element subsets of I) with non-concurrent lines there is a triangle K_J, and the axioms (A5), (A6) concern an orientation omega_J of K_J.

The page continues the '2nd case' from the previous page: every pseudoline of the system passes through one of the three vertices a,b,c of K_J. Choose lines D_{a_i} (from I minus J) through the vertices a_i, with the three not concurrent. Here a_i is the vertex opposite D_i. This gives a 6-line configuration with 9 points:
- the triple points a_i;
- alpha_i = D_{a_i} meet D_i;
- a'_i = D_{a_j} meet D_{a_k}.

Each cevian D_{a_i} carries four points: a_i, alpha_i, a'_j, a'_k. On a projective line the cyclic order of 4 points is fixed (up to reversal) by saying which point is 'opposite' (non-adjacent) to a_i. So the 1-dimensional structure of the configuration is completely given by these three choices.

Claim: if the figure comes from a 2-dimensional arrangement, exactly one of two cases occurs.
- Case I: there is a unique cyclic order on J such that a_i is opposite a'_{i+1} on D_{a_i}. In the drawn figure this order is abc.
- Case II (margin): for every i, a_i is opposite alpha_i.

Each cevian D_{a_i}, the line through alpha_i, induces an orientation lambda_i of K_J. Grothendieck states that the three lambda_i are mutually compatible in case I and incompatible in case II.

Axiom (A6), finished on the next page, then demands two things for every such choice of three non-concurrent cevians:
- (1) the 6-line 1-dimensional configuration is of type I or II;
- (2) the orientation of K_J defined by the rule (via the lambda_i, corrected in case II) is independent of the choice of cevians.

The next page treats the remaining case, where all supplementary lines are concurrent. This forces card I = 6, giving the complete-quadrilateral-type arrangement with 4 triple points, related to a V_4 colouring.

Purpose: a local, finite set of axioms (orientations of triangles plus compatibility on small subconfigurations) characterising pseudoline arrangements through their 1-dimensional 'polygonal' data. In modern terms this is a rank-3 oriented matroid / chirotope or local-sequence characterisation.
errors: The transcription's margin note 'a_i soit opposé à a'_i' cannot be right, since a'_i does not lie on D_{a_i}. It must read alpha_i.

The claim that a realisable configuration is always of type I or II is asserted without proof. Spot checks with straight lines bear it out: interior cevians and mixed interior/exterior cevians give case I; the anticomplementary-type configuration with cevians parallel to the opposite sides gives case II. A full proof for pseudolines is not on the page.

The phrase 'non compatible dans le cas II' leaves implicit how the orientation of K_J is then defined. Presumably it is by a fixed correction rule; this is only clarified on the next page ('la prescription précédente').

ideas.what: Encoding the 1-dimensional structure of a pseudoline configuration by the cyclic order (separation / 'opposite' relation) of points on each line, and asking which such data come from a 2-dimensional arrangement
ideas.modern_name: local sequences / allowable sequences; realisability of local sequences as pseudoline arrangements

ideas.what: Orientation omega_J attached to each triangle K_J (J a 3-subset of the lines), with consistency axioms (A5), (A6)
ideas.modern_name: chirotope of a rank-3 oriented matroid / Knuth's CC-systems

ideas.what: Classification of the 6-line 'triangle plus three non-concurrent cevians' configuration into two types (I: cyclic 'rotation' type; II: each vertex opposite the foot of its cevian), and using it to transport triangle orientations
ideas.modern_name: Ceva/Menelaus-type sign configurations; small forbidden/allowed subconfigurations in local-sequence characterisations
ideas.usually_credited_to: classical (Ceva/Menelaus); combinatorial version implicit in oriented-matroid literature

missed.claim: Grothendieck attempts an axiomatisation of NON-simple pseudoline arrangements (with multiple points) directly from 1-dimensional data. The data are incidences plus polygonal structure on the lines, together with triangle orientations whose consistency is tested on small 6-line subconfigurations (types I/II). It is unclear whether this finite local system of axioms is equivalent to known characterisations (chirotope axioms, Felsner–Weil signotopes, Streinu's local sequences).
missed.quote: on exige (1°) que l'ens. 1-dim. K_{J'} des 6 droites obtenues soit dans un cas (I) ou (II) ci-dessus, et (2°) que l'orientation de K_J ... ne dépende pas du choix de J'
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A minor historical precursor (c. 1981) of 'local sequence' characterisations of pseudoline arrangements in the non-simple case. Comparing it with the oriented-matroid axioms could be a modest historical note, but it is unlikely to yield new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is an interesting but routine-level step in an independent rediscovery, around 1981, of chirotope/local-sequence-style axioms for pseudoline arrangements, an area developed by Goodman–Pollack, Folkman–Lawrence and Knuth. Grothendieck's work on pseudolines is little known, and the non-simple local approach is mildly notable. The specific content (a two-case classification of a Ceva-type 6-line configuration) is elementary.
